passage:
The waiting area of the bank branch smelled of floor cleaner. Naveen took a token and waited an hour before Suraj, the customer service executive, glanced up.

"Fraud? A ticket will be raised. Wait for the email," Suraj said, without looking at the papers Naveen had brought. Naveen felt hot with irritation and a helpless sinking.

"Could I have the ticket number in writing, please?"

A printed slip came out. A week later there was still no reply. Naveen sat down with a folder: the slip, screenshots, transaction details, the dates of every call. A formal complaint went out by email, with a stamped copy handed in at the branch. When the promised time passed, Naveen escalated to the bank's nodal officer and noted the ombudsman as the next step if it stalled.

Slowly the answers came. "Not warm," Naveen told a friend, "but paper works."

qa.q: What did Naveen ask Suraj to provide in writing?
qa.a: Naveen asked for the ticket number in writing.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about the response at the counter?
qa.a: Naveen felt hot with irritation and a helpless sinking, as Suraj did not even look at the papers.

qa.q: What could Naveen do if the nodal officer's reply also stalls?
qa.a: Keep the folder organised, follow up in writing, and escalate to the ombudsman as already noted.

qa.q: What might it be like for Suraj at that counter?
qa.a: Suraj may be handling a long queue of routine tickets, which could explain the flat reply, though the passage does not say why Suraj was so brief.

grounding: After a fraud, the bank's support is slow and cold; Naveen stays organised with written complaints and escalation.

passage:
Legal-aid volunteer's note, Wednesday.
Zainab came to the clinic with a thick folder. Three weeks ago, fifty thousand was taken from her account through a fake app. She reported it to her bank the same day. Since then, the helpline has told her "under process" four times. The last agent, Thomas, said, "Ma'am, there's nothing more I can do," and ended the call.
She was tired but not giving up. She had kept every complaint number, the dates of each call and screenshots.
We wrote a formal complaint letter to the bank's grievance officer with the timeline attached, and I explained that if there was no satisfactory reply in the time the bank's rules allow, she could escalate to the banking ombudsman. She also filed on the cybercrime portal, which she had not yet done.
She left calmer, with a checklist of follow-up dates. We'll review her reply together.

qa.q: How many times did the helpline say "under process"?
What was Zainab feeling when she came to the clinic?
qa.a: She was tired and frustrated by the cold responses, but still determined not to give up.

qa.q: What steps did the volunteer help Zainab take?
qa.a: Writing a formal complaint to the bank's grievance officer with a timeline, filing on the cybercrime portal, and planning escalation to the banking ombudsman if needed.

qa.q: How might Thomas, the helpline agent, see Zainab's case?
qa.a: Thomas may feel it is out of his hands and move on, not seeing how the cold reply adds to her stress.

grounding: After fraud, the bank's support is slow and cold; the protagonist stays persistent and organised with written complaints and escalation.

passage:
Indu's diary, day 19.
Another call to the payment platform's support line. 42 minutes on hold. The agent read out the same script: "Your case is being reviewed." I asked for the case officer's name. "Not available." I wanted to scream.
Jeevan came over with dinner and found me with my head on the table. "Just forget it, it's gone," he said. I nearly agreed.
But then I opened my notes. Nineteen days of dates, reference numbers, names.
Things I did tonight:
- wrote a formal email to the platform's grievance officer, with all the reference numbers attached
- printed the timeline so I don't have to remember it in my head
- set a reminder: if no proper answer by the date in their policy, escalate to the ombudsman
- filed the cybercrime report number in the same folder
Still angry. But organised angry. Jeevan is helping me make a tracking sheet. Not despairing.

qa.q: How long was Indu on hold today?
How did Indu feel after the call?
qa.a: Indu felt frustrated and close to despair, wanting to scream, before choosing to get organised.

qa.q: What did Indu do to put documented pressure on the platform?
qa.a: Indu emailed the grievance officer with all reference numbers, printed a timeline, set a reminder to escalate to the ombudsman, and filed everything together.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see Indu's persistence?
qa.a: Jeevan first thought it was hopeless, but he seems to come round, helping make a tracking sheet.

grounding: After fraud a platform's support is slow and cold; the protagonist stays persistent and organised, using written complaints and planned escalation.
